meta.title: Who really said "Beauty is the promise of happiness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Edmund Burke. Stendhal wrote it in a footnote to De l'Amour (1822), ch. 17 - and his line was "Beauty is only the promise of happiness."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beauty is the promise of happiness'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Edmund Burke. It's Stendhal, De l'Amour (1822), ch. 17, footnote - and the popular version quietly drops his word "only."

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — actually Stendhal
answer.authorDates: 1783–1842 · French novelist, pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle
answer.sourceLine: The line is Stendhal’s, from a footnote in chapter 17 of De l’Amour (1822): “La beauté n’est que la promesse du bonheur.” Edmund Burke never wrote it — he died in 1797, twenty-five years before the book appeared — and the popular English wording is itself a trimmed one: the 1915 Woolf translation reads “Beauty is only the promise of happiness.”

source.heading: The footnote it comes from

docMeta.dd: Chapter 17, “La beauté détrônée par l’amour” — footnote
Philip Sidney Woolf & Cecil N. Sidney Woolf, On Love (New York: Brentano’s, first published 1915)

source.excerpt:
If ugliness thus comes to be preferred and loved, it is because in this case ugliness is beauty.[1] …

[1] Beauty is only the promise of happiness. The happiness of a Greek was different to that of a Frenchman of 1822. See the eyes of the Medici Venus and compare them with the eyes of the Magdalen of Pordenone (in the possession of M. de Sommariva.)
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Stendhal entry ↗ files the line under De L’Amour (1822), “Ch. 17, footnote,” giving the French “La beauté n’est que la promesse du bonheur” and rendering it “Beauty is nothing other than the promise of happiness.”

The footnote is present in the French text itself: chapter 17 in the 1927 Martineau edition ↗ and, independently, the 1853 Lévy edition page scan ↗, both reading “La beauté n’est que la promesse du bonheur.”

In English, the Woolf brothers’ translation ↗ carries it as footnote 1 to the chapter “Beauty Dethroned by Love”: “Beauty is only the promise of happiness.” A scan of the 1915 Brentano’s printing ↗ is on the Internet Archive.

Nothing ties it to Burke: a full-text check of the Gutenberg volume of Burke’s Writings and Speeches containing his Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful ↗ returns no occurrence of “promise of happiness.”
source.excerptNote: English as it stands in the Woolf brothers’ 1915 translation. The French original reads: “La beauté n’est que la promesse du bonheur. Le bonheur d’un Grec était différent du bonheur d’un Français de 1822.”

author.name: Stendhal
author.heading: Who was Stendhal?
author.metaLine: 1783–1842 · French novelist & critic, pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle
author.bio: Marie-Henri Beyle, who published as Stendhal, was born in Grenoble in 1783 and died in Paris in 1842. He is best remembered for the novels Le Rouge et le Noir (The Red and the Black, 1830) and La Chartreuse de Parme (The Charterhouse of Parma, 1839). De l’Amour, the 1822 essay in which this footnote sits, was largely ignored on publication but is now read as one of the first modern attempts to analyse love as psychology — it is the book that introduced his idea of “crystallization.”

misattribution.heading: How Burke ended up with Stendhal’s footnote
misattribution.intro: Edmund Burke is one of the internet’s standing magnets for unsourced aphorisms, and a line about beauty is an especially easy fit because Burke really did write the era’s most famous English treatise on the subject. But the sentence is not his, and the wording that circulates is not quite Stendhal’s either.

items.why: Quote aggregators list the line under Burke with no work, page or date attached — see Quotefancy ↗ and The Socratic Method ↗, neither of which cites a source or mentions Stendhal. A full-text search of the Gutenberg volume of Burke’s Writings and Speeches that contains his Enquiry on the Sublime and Beautiful ↗ finds no instance of “promise of happiness,” and Wikiquote’s Burke page ↗ lists the line only in its Misattributed section, correcting it to Stendhal, De L’Amour (1822), ch. 17.

Stendhal’s French is “La beauté n’est que la promesse du bonheur” — beauty is nothing but a promise. The 1915 translation keeps that limit: “Beauty is only the promise of happiness” ↗. The exact string “Beauty is the promise of happiness” does not occur in that translation; dropping “only” turns a demotion of beauty into a tribute to it.

In On the Genealogy of Morals, third essay §6 ↗, Nietzsche writes that Stendhal “once called the beautiful une promesse de bonheur” — his own shorter formulation, and the form in which the line entered aesthetic debate.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to Stendhal, in a footnote to chapter 17 of De l’Amour (1822) — verifiable in the French at the 1853 Lévy edition page scan ↗ and in Wikiquote’s sourced Stendhal entry ↗.

context.heading: Beauty dethroned, not crowned
lead: The chapter this footnote hangs from is titled “Beauty Dethroned by Love.” Stendhal is not paying beauty a compliment — he is cutting it down to size. His argument is that a lover will prefer a plainer face that promises a hundred units of happiness to a more beautiful one that promises three, and that beauty therefore has no value of its own: it is only a forecast, and a culturally local one at that. The footnote spells this out by adding that “the happiness of a Greek was different to that of a Frenchman of 1822,” pointing the reader at the eyes of the Medici Venus versus those of Pordenone’s Magdalen.

Strip out the word “only” — as the internet version does — and the sentence flips into an inspirational compliment to beauty, which is close to the opposite of what the chapter is arguing. That trimmed form is the one that ends up on posters under Edmund Burke’s name.
context.detailsSummary: How Nietzsche carried the line into philosophy
detailsBody: The phrase became famous in aesthetics largely through Friedrich Nietzsche, who set it against Kant. In the third essay, section 6 of On the Genealogy of Morals, Nietzsche contrasts Kant’s “that is beautiful which pleases without interesting” with a definition “made by a real ‘spectator’ and ‘artist’ — by Stendhal, who once called the beautiful une promesse de bonheur.”
Nietzsche’s French is his own compression rather than Stendhal’s sentence, and it is that shortened form — “a promise of happiness,” with no “only” — that most later English quoters inherited.
context.pull: “Only” is the whole argument. Delete it and Stendhal starts saying the reverse.
